content: Several factors can influence the progression of normal labor. It has been hypothesized that administering intravenous (IV) fluids routinely during labor to maintain adequate hydration may reduce the duration of uterine contractions and relaxation, potentially shortening the overall length of labor. Additionally, it has been suggested that IV fluids might decrease the rate of cesarean sections (CS) performed for prolonged labor. However, despite its widespread use, the routine administration of IV fluids during labor has not been thoroughly studied, and there is no consensus on the type or volume of fluids required, or even whether IV fluids are necessary at all. Women may be able to maintain adequate hydration through oral intake during labor. Furthermore, excessive IV fluid administration may pose risks to both the mother and the newborn, with different types of fluids carrying distinct risks. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether the routine administration of IV fluids to low-risk, first-time mothers in labor reduces the duration of labor and to assess the safety of IV fluids for both maternal and neonatal health. The review included nine randomized controlled trials involving 1,781 women. Some trials had multiple treatment arms and were included in more than one comparison. Two trials compared women who received up to 250 mL/hour of Ringer's lactate solution along with oral intake versus oral intake alone. Among women who delivered vaginally, those in the Ringer's lactate group experienced a reduction in labor duration (mean difference [MD] -28.86 minutes, 95% confidence interval [CI] -47.41 to -10.30). However, there was no statistically significant reduction in the number of cesarean sections in this group (risk ratio [RR] 0.73, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.08). Three trials compared women who received 125 mL/hour versus 250 mL/hour of IV fluids, with both groups allowed free oral intake. Women receiving the higher volume of IV fluids (250 mL/hour) had shorter labors compared to those receiving 125 mL/hour (MD -23.87 minutes, 95% CI -3.72 to -44.02, 256 women). However, there was no statistically significant reduction in cesarean section rates in the 250 mL/hour group (average RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.87, three studies, 334 women). In one study, the rate of assisted vaginal deliveries was lower in the group receiving 125 mL/hour (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.27 to 0.81). Four trials compared IV fluid rates in women with restricted oral intake (125 mL/hour versus 250 mL/hour). Women receiving the higher infusion rate (250 mL/hour) experienced a significant reduction in labor duration (MD -105.61 minutes, 95% CI -53.19 to -158.02; P < 0.0001). However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously due to high heterogeneity among trials (I² = 53%). There was a significant reduction in cesarean section rates in the higher infusion rate group (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.10 to 2.21; P = 0.01). No differences were observed in the rate of assisted vaginal deliveries (RR 0.78, 95% CI 0.44 to 1.40) or in the number of newborns admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.07 to 3.17). Two trials compared normal saline with 5% dextrose. Only one trial reported the mean duration of labor, and there was no strong evidence of a difference between groups (MD -12.00 minutes, 95% CI -30.09 to 6.09). However, a trial reporting the median duration suggested that labor was shorter in the dextrose group. There were no significant differences in cesarean section rates (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.43, two studies, 284 women) or assisted vaginal delivery rates (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.21 to 1.63, one study, 93 women). One trial reported maternal hyponatremia (serum sodium levels < 135 mmol/L). Regarding neonatal outcomes, there were no differences in NICU admissions or low Apgar scores. However, 33.3% of newborns in the dextrose group developed hyponatremia compared to 13.3% in the normal saline group (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.93; P = 0.03). One trial also reported a higher incidence of neonatal hyperbilirubinemia in the dextrose group. No differences were observed in neonatal hypoglycemia between groups. The authors concluded that while IV fluid administration compared to oral intake alone was associated with a reduction in labor duration, this finding was based on only two trials. Other trials suggested that in cases where oral intake is restricted, administering IV fluids at a rate of 250 mL/hour rather than 125 mL/hour may shorten labor duration in first-time mothers. However, it may be possible for women to increase their oral intake instead of being attached to an IV drip, raising questions about the necessity of a nil by mouth policy. Concerns about the safety of dextrose solutions were highlighted and warrant further investigation. None of the trials evaluated maternal perspectives on being attached to an IV drip throughout labor, nor did they objectively assess dehydration. The evidence from this review does not provide strong support for the routine use of IV fluids during labor. Interpretation of the results was limited by the small number of trials, variability between trials, and inconsistent findings. Additionally, important outcomes related to maternal and neonatal health were often not reported.
